newsitem.title: CANADA: ICAO wants talks on Cuba overflights of U.S..
newsitem.headline: ICAO wants talks on Cuba overflights of U.S..

text.p: The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) said on Thursday it had asked the United States and Cuba to resume direct talks on allowing Cuban-registered planes to fly over U.S. territory on flights to and from Canada.

The Montreal-based U.N.-affiliated agency said the ICAO Council had designated its president, Assad Kotaite, as conciliator in the negotiations and has set a deadline of autumn 1997 for the talks. Kotaite will present progress reports on the negotiations from March 1997.
Kotaite told Reuters his preliminary discussions with Washington had produced "very, very slight progress."
"I am hopeful that I will be able to return with a positive report," he said.

Kotaite said any decision by ICAO's council could be the subject of an appeal to international courts by either country. This is only the third time in its 52-year history that ICAO has been asked to conciliate in such a dispute.
In 1967, the agency was asked to help resolve a dispute between Britain and Spain on airspace over Gibraltor. In 1971, it helped Pakistan and India to resolve a similar squabble.

ICAO said its decision to act as conciliator between Cuba and the United States related to an application for settlement filed by the Cuban government under the agency's rules for the settlement of differences.

The application referred to a disagreement over the interpretation and application of the International Air Services Transit Agreement and to the Convention on International Civil Aviation, ICAO said.
The U.S. government bans direct flights to Cuba from the United States. Since 1980, it has also banned the overflight of U.S. territory by Cuban-registered planes on flights between Cuba and Canada.

Cuban officials have complained that flights by Cuba's national carrier Cubana Airlines between Havana and Montreal and Toronto take much longer because they are not allowed to fly over U.S. territory. Earlier this year, Cuba threatened to prevent U.S. commercial airplanes from flying through Cuban airspace, but took no action.
